noticeAndWonder.context: Engineers on Station Helios need to break 84 replacement circuit boards into equal shipping crates, and the crates must be built using only prime-numbered groupings. Start splitting 84 into two factors: 84 = 2 × 42. Then 42 = 2 × 21, and 21 = 3 × 7. What do you notice about how each split works, and what do you wonder about how you'll know when the factor tree is finished?
wonderStarters: I wonder what would happen if…

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Trophy Case Display
revealWordProblem.text: The school trophy case has 84 trophies to arrange on shelves. The display designer wants to break 84 down into its prime factors first, then use those primes to decide how many equal-sized groups of trophies she can create. What is the prime factorization of 84, written both as a product of primes and using exponents? Show each step of your factor tree.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: 84 = 2 × 42. Since 42 is not prime, split it: 42 = 2 × 21. Since 21 is not prime, split it: 21 = 3 × 7. Both 3 and 7 are prime, so the tree is done. The prime factorization of 84 is 2 × 2 × 3 × 7, which can be written with exponents as 2² × 3 × 7. Check: 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 = 4 × 3 × 7 = 12 × 7 = 84. Correct.

vocabulary.definition: A number bigger than 1 that you can only divide by 1 and itself.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un número mayor que 1 que solo se puede dividir entre 1 y sí mismo.
vocabulary.visual: 7 has only two factors: 1 × 7. So 7 is prime.
vocabulary.cloze: A whole number greater than 1 with exactly two factors, 1 and itself, is a ___ number.

examples.why: 9 = 3 × 3, so it has more than two factors.
1 has only one factor, so it is not prime.

vocabulary.definition: A number bigger than 1 that you can divide by more than just 1 and itself.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un número mayor que 1 que se puede dividir entre más números, no solo 1 y sí mismo.
vocabulary.cloze: A whole number greater than 1 that has more than two factors is a ___ number.

examples.why: 15 = 3 × 5, so it has more than two factors.
5 is prime; it has only two factors.
2 is prime; its only factors are 1 and 2.

vocabulary.definition: Writing a number as prime numbers multiplied together.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Escribir un número como números primos multiplicados.

vocabulary.definition: A factor of a whole number divides it evenly, with no remainder. For example, 3 is a factor of 12 because 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un factor de un número entero lo divide exactamente, sin dejar residuo. Por ejemplo, 3 es un factor de 12 porque 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
vocabulary.cloze: A number that divides evenly into another number is called a ___.

examples.why: 12 ÷ 5 = 2 remainder 2, so 5 does not divide 12 evenly.

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — What is prime factorization?
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. In this group we go deeper: trickier numbers, a second way to see it, and explaining why it works — not just getting the answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Keep breaking a number apart until every factor is a prime number you cannot split anymore — and you can explain why it works, even when it gets tricky.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: I want the prime factorization of 60. I start by splitting it: 60 = 6 × 10.
6 is not prime, so I break it: 6 = 2 × 3. Both 2 and 3 are prime, so I stop those branches.
10 is not prime, so I break it: 10 = 2 × 5. Both 2 and 5 are prime, so I stop.
Using exponents, I write it as 2² × 3 × 5. I check: 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 60. Correct.

onLevel.stem: Two students found different factor trees for 60. Student A started with 2 × 30. Student B started with 6 × 10. Which statement is true?
choices: Both get the same prime factorization: 2 × 2 × 3 × 5
Only Student A gets the correct prime factorization
Only Student B gets the correct prime factorization
They will get different prime factorizations
onLevel.explanation: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says every composite number has exactly one prime factorization. No matter how you start the factor tree, you always end with 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.
choiceFeedback: Try listing the factors again—check each one.
hints: Notice the question isn't asking which START is right — it asks what happens when both finished trees are compared.
Finish BOTH trees yourself: keep splitting every branch down to primes, then compare the two final lists of prime factors.
Student A: 60 = 2 × 30, then 30 = 2 × 15, then 15 = 3 × 5. Now finish Student B's tree from 6 × 10 and compare the prime lists.

onLevel.title: Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Find the prime factorization of 45, using exponents

onLevel.correctWork: 45 = 5 × 3 × 3 has one 5 and two 3's — not two 5's. The exponent on a prime factor shows how many times that factor appears, so the correct form is 45 = 3² × 5 (the 5 has no exponent shown because it appears only once).
hints: Count how many times each prime factor actually appears in the factor tree before you write its exponent.
5 only appears once in 45 = 3 × 3 × 5, so its exponent is 1 (usually left off) — not 2.

onLevel.title: Find Marcus's Mistake
onLevel.correctWork: 8 = 2 × 4, but 4 is not prime. 4 = 2 × 2, so 8 = 2 × 2 × 2. The correct prime factorization is 48 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2⁴ × 3.
hints: Look at Step 4 — is every factor in the answer a prime number?
4 is not prime because 4 = 2 × 2. Marcus needed to keep breaking it down.

onLevel.prompt: Choose any two-digit composite number. Show TWO different factor trees that both lead to the same prime factorization. Explain why every composite number has only one prime factorization.
onLevel.sentenceFrame: I chose the number ___. My first factor tree starts with ___ × ___, and my second starts with ___ × ___. Both give the same prime factorization: ___. This happens because ___.
hints: Re-read the task: pick ONE two-digit composite number (like 24, 36, or 40) and build TWO trees with different first splits.
Choose two different starting pairs for your number — for 36 you could start with 4 × 9 or 6 × 6 — and finish both trees to primes.
Say you pick 24: tree one starts 2 × 12, tree two starts 4 × 6. Finish both, list each tree's primes, and explain why the lists match.

extending.stem: The first lock panel shows 90. What is the prime factorization of 90?
extending.explanation: 90 = 2 × 45 = 2 × 9 × 5 = 2 × 3 × 3 × 5. Every factor is prime, so the lock accepts 2 × 3 × 3 × 5.
choiceFeedback: Check if every factor in that product is actually prime.

extending.stem: The second panel needs a number whose prime factorization is 2² × 3². Which number unlocks it?
extending.explanation: 2² × 3² = 4 × 9 = 36, so 36 is the code for this panel.
choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.

extending.stem: The final lock asks for the prime factorization of 78 written as a product of primes. Which is correct?
extending.explanation: 78 = 2 × 39 = 2 × 3 × 13. All three factors are prime, so 2 × 3 × 13 unlocks the final panel.
choiceFeedback: Check if every factor in that product is actually prime.

extending.title: Level 2 Extension — Fix the Broken Factor Tree
extending.correctWork: 12 = 2 × 6, but 6 is not prime. 6 = 2 × 3, so 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. The complete prime factorization is 96 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2⁵ × 3.
hints: Check every factor in the final answer — is 6 a prime number?
6 is composite because 6 = 2 × 3, so the tree must keep splitting until every branch is prime.

extending.stem: Which of the following is a prime number?
extending.explanation: 17 has exactly two factors: 1 and 17. 15 = 3 × 5, 21 = 3 × 7, and 9 = 3 × 3, so they are all composite.
choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
hints: Re-read what 'prime' means: exactly two factors, 1 and itself. Any extra factor makes a number composite.
Test each choice by dividing by small primes like 2, 3, 5, and 7. If anything divides in evenly, that number is composite.
Start with 9: since 3 × 3 = 9, it has a factor besides 1 and 9, so 9 is composite. Cross it off and test the next choice the same way.

extending.stem: What is the prime factorization of 30?
extending.explanation: 30 = 2 × 15 = 2 × 3 × 5. All three factors (2, 3, 5) are prime, so 2 × 3 × 5 is the prime factorization.
choiceFeedback: Check if every factor in that product is actually prime.
hints: A prime factorization uses ONLY prime numbers. Look at each choice: are ALL of its factors prime?
Break 30 down step by step, and keep splitting any factor that is still composite until every factor is prime.
Start with 30 = 2 × 15. Is 15 prime? No — so split 15 into two primes and collect everything you found.

extending.stem: What is the prime factorization of 18?
extending.explanation: 18 = 2 × 9 = 2 × 3 × 3. Both 2 and 3 are prime, so 2 × 3 × 3 is the prime factorization.
choiceFeedback: Check if every factor in that product is actually prime.
hints: Check every factor in each choice — numbers like 9 and 6 are composite, so they can't appear in a prime factorization.
Build a factor tree for 18: split it into two factors, then keep splitting anything composite until only primes remain.
Begin with 18 = 2 × 9. The 9 isn't prime, so break 9 into two equal prime factors and list all the primes you end with.

extending.stem: Which of these numbers is composite?
extending.explanation: 27 = 3 × 9 = 3 × 3 × 3, so it has more than two factors. 23, 29, and 31 are all prime.
choiceFeedback: Try listing the factors again—check each one.
hints: Composite means MORE than two factors. Ask for each number: can I split it into two smaller whole numbers?
Try dividing each choice by small primes like 2, 3, and 5. A digit-sum divisible by 3 means the whole number divides by 3.
Test 23 first: try 2, 3, and 5 — none divide it evenly, so 23 is prime. Cross it off and test the other numbers the same way.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Prime Factorization is stopping the factor tree too soon — leaving a composite number like 4, 6, 8, or 9 in the final answer instead of continuing to split it. For example, writing 20 = 4 × 5 as the prime factorization (4 is composite) instead of finishing with 20 = 2 × 2 × 5. Before you submit, check every number in your final answer: if any factor can still be broken into smaller factors, the tree isn't finished yet.

connect.scenario: A station gardener is loading 72 seed pods into the greenhouse and wants to build a perfectly rectangular planting grid. Starting from the prime factorization of 72, she combines the prime factors to list every factor of 72 and choose a grid that uses all the pods.

connect.prompt: Because 72 = ___, I can multiply combinations of those prime factors to get factors like ___, so a grid that works is ___ by ___.

exitTicket.stem: Explain your thinking — What is the prime factorization of 40?
exitTicket.hint: Think through the problem step by step.
choiceFeedback: 4 and 10 aren't prime — keep splitting until every factor is prime.
8 isn't prime — break it down further into primes.
20 still breaks down — a prime factorization stops only at primes.
hints: A prime factorization keeps going until EVERY factor is prime — factors like 4, 8, 10, and 20 still need splitting.
Build a factor tree for 40 and keep splitting every composite branch until only prime numbers are left at the ends.
Start with 40 = 4 × 10. Split the 4 into 2 × 2, then split the 10 into primes — then collect every prime at the ends of the branches.

Empieza probando la divisibilidad entre 2, luego entre 3 y luego entre 5.
Empieza así: El factor primo más pequeño de 129 es 3.
parallelPractice.explanationEs: El factor primo más pequeño de 129 es 3. 129 ÷ 3 = 43. Sigue separando hasta que cada número del final sea primo. Escribe la factorización prima: 3 × 43.

steps.prompt: The smallest prime factor of 134 is ___.
steps.promptEs: El factor primo más pequeño de 134 es ___.

steps.prompt: Keep splitting until every end number is prime. Write the prime factorization: ___.
steps.promptEs: Sigue separando hasta que cada número del final sea primo. Escribe la factorización prima: ___.

hints: Re-read the question. What exactly is it asking you to find?

Start like this: The smallest prime factor of 134 is 2.
parallelPractice.explanation: The smallest prime factor of 134 is 2. 134 ÷ 2 = 67. Keep splitting until every end number is prime. Write the prime factorization: 2 × 67.

questions.stem: Which of these numbers is composite?
questions.explanation: 27 = 3 × 9 = 3 × 3 × 3, so it has more than two factors. 23, 29, and 31 are all prime.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a prime number?
questions.explanation: 17 has exactly two factors: 1 and 17. 15 = 3 × 5, 21 = 3 × 7, and 9 = 3 × 3, so they are all composite.

questions.stem: What is the prime factorization of 18?
questions.explanation: 18 = 2 × 9 = 2 × 3 × 3. Both 2 and 3 are prime, so 2 × 3 × 3 is the prime factorization.

questions.stem: What is the prime factorization of 30?
questions.explanation: 30 = 2 × 15 = 2 × 3 × 5. All three factors (2, 3, 5) are prime, so 2 × 3 × 5 is the prime factorization.
